Overview

OpenAI explains why it took ChatGPT offline on Monday, 20 March 2023. A bug in redis-py, the open-source Python client for Redis, let some users see the titles of another active user's chat history, and possibly the first message of a new conversation. The same bug may have exposed payment details of 1.2% of ChatGPT Plus subscribers active during a nine-hour window: name, email address, payment address, the last four digits of a card number and its expiry date, though never a full card number. That could happen through subscription confirmation emails sent to the wrong users between 1 a.m. and 10 a.m. Pacific time, or on the "Manage my subscription" page in the same window. OpenAI caches user information in Redis Cluster and reaches it through redis-py from an asyncio Python server. The client shares a pool of connections. If a request was cancelled after it was sent but before its response was read, the connection was left corrupted, and the next, unrelated request on it could receive the leftover data. Usually that caused a server error, but sometimes the data had the expected type and was returned as valid. A server change at 1 a.m. on 20 March caused a spike in cancellations. OpenAI sent the maintainers a patch and lists its own actions: testing the fix, redundant checks that cached data belongs to the requesting user, a programmatic log review, identifying and notifying affected users, better logging, and a sturdier Redis cluster. Chat history was restored except for a few hours.

Implementations

Searched on 2026-11-02. None applies: this is an incident report. The bug was in redis-py (MIT, https://github.com/redis/redis-py). NVD tracks it as CVE-2023-28858 (redis-py before 4.5.3; releases 4.3.6, 4.4.3 and 4.5.3 changed pipeline behaviour), whose record cites this post and says it was first created in response to reports about ChatGPT, and as CVE-2023-28859 (fixed in 4.4.4 and 4.5.4), which addresses data leakage across asyncio connections in general. The post itself names no CVE or version.

Limits

  • Read from an archive. openai.com returned HTTP 403 to scripted requests on 2026-11-02. The digest is of the Internet Archive's copy from two days after publication; the live page may have changed.
  • Hedged numbers. OpenAI believes very few users' data "was actually revealed to someone else" but gives no count beyond the 1.2% share; exposure before 20 March is called possible but unconfirmed.
  • The provider's own account. No independent investigation is cited.
  • "Outage" undersells it. The title names the downtime; the substance is a data exposure.
